Business Situation (1-2 lines): A 12-year duty manager corners you in the backroom and says your allocation plan won't work, citing experience.
Primary Decision: You hold the decision rights but they have more store experience. How do you respond?
Options (A-D): A) Hold the line and explain your rationale  B) Ask what specifically they're seeing that you might be missing  C) Defer to their judgement and adopt their plan  D) Invite them to refine the plan with you in five minutes
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Veteran feels heard, plan is sharpened with shop-floor reality, leadership consistency intact
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Either you bulldoze a credible voice (trust drops) or you cave entirely (consistency drops, plan still wrong)

Business Situation (1-2 lines): A new assistant manager pulls you aside about a flare-up between two team leaders over the rota, asking whether to step in.
Primary Decision: A new leader is asking for your view. How do you respond?
Options (A-D): A) Give them your answer so they can act on it  B) Ask them what the risks of each choice are  C) Tell them the decision is theirs and you'll back it  D) Offer to think it through with them for ten minutes
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Alex builds judgement muscle, learns to weigh trade-offs, capability uplift carries forward
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Either you do their thinking for them (capability stalls) or you abandon them (decision quality suffers)

Business Situation (1-2 lines): A capable shift supervisor has missed two briefings this week. Team leaders are starting to question whether briefings matter.
Primary Decision: You need to land this conversation well. How do you open it?
Options (A-D): A) Be clear that briefings are non-negotiable  B) Ask what's getting in the way and what support is needed  C) Ask them what they want to commit to  D) Revisit the briefing format together
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Root cause surfaces, performance recovers without the team feeling threatened, briefings restored
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Pattern entrenches, team reads it as the standard slipping, leadership consistency erodes

Business Situation (1-2 lines): A top-performing team leader tells you she's been offered a competitor role and feels she's "treading water".
Primary Decision: A top performer is on the verge of leaving. How do you respond?
Options (A-D): A) Lay out what you can realistically offer  B) Ask her what 'treading water' actually looks like  C) Tell her you trust her to weigh it up  D) Offer to co-design what the next 90 days look like
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Priya stays, growth path is co-owned, retention signal strengthens across the team
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Star colleague exits, knock-on attrition risk, capability hit you can't replace quickly

Business Situation (1-2 lines): An assistant manager passed over for promotion delivers a flat "whatever you think" to a junior, who visibly deflates.
Primary Decision: You've been letting this pattern slide. How do you handle it?
Options (A-D): A) Pull Dan aside and name the behaviour  B) Ask Dan how his responses are landing  C) Have the junior feed back to Dan directly  D) Sit with Dan and talk honestly about the last few months
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Honest conversation rebuilds connection, behaviour shifts, junior colleagues stop being collateral
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Resentment compounds, others learn the bar has dropped, engagement leaks

Business Situation (1-2 lines): A team leader asks for shift flexibility for personal reasons, but it would strain a rota others just accepted.
Primary Decision: The fair-process question is live. How do you handle it?
Options (A-D): A) Decline to protect equity  B) Ask Mia what a fair outcome looks like  C) Approve and trust her to manage fallout  D) Co-design a solution that could extend to others
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Need is met without breaking fairness, principle scales to future cases, trust both ways
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Either Mia feels unsupported or the wider team senses favouritism - either way leadership consistency takes a hit

Business Situation (1-2 lines): A team leader has watched a colleague under-ring discounted items for friends three times. He's only just spoken up.
Primary Decision: Ben is asking you to take the next step. How do you respond?
Options (A-D): A) Take it from here, loss prevention picks it up  B) Ask what made this the moment he spoke up  C) Tell him he's done right and ask how he wants it handled  D) Walk through the process so he knows what happens next
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Ben is supported, process is followed cleanly, future speak-ups become more likely
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Whistleblower regrets coming forward, process feels opaque, theft pattern continues unchecked

Business Situation (1-2 lines): You gave Kate feedback this morning. She nodded but has been cool all afternoon, ahead of a planning session together.
Primary Decision: The feedback didn't land the way you intended. How do you reopen it?
Options (A-D): A) Push on with the planning session, performance stands  B) Check in: ask how the feedback sat overnight  C) Leave her space and trust her to raise it  D) Name what you're noticing and offer to replay the conversation
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Working relationship recovers, feedback lands properly the second time, planning session is honest
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Resentment hardens, future feedback is rejected before it's heard, working relationship cools further

Business Situation (1-2 lines): An assistant manager has quietly covered two team leader roles for a fortnight. Stays 90 minutes late, says she's "fine".
Primary Decision: You know what's coming. What stance do you walk in with?
Options (A-D): A) Get ahead of it, tell her what you're taking off her plate  B) Ask what 'fine' has actually looked like  C) Hand her the choice of what to drop  D) Sit down together and rebuild the coverage plan
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Workload is recalibrated jointly, burnout averted, Nadia learns to flag earlier next time
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Burnout, sickness absence, you lose her temporarily or permanently right when you can least afford it

Business Situation (1-2 lines): A team leader two weeks back from long-term sick directly asks: "I feel like I'm being handled. Am I?"
Primary Decision: It's a direct question. How do you respond?
Options (A-D): A) Be straight - yes, the team has been cautious, here's what changes  B) Ask him what being handled feels like from where he stands  C) Tell him his team will take their cue from him  D) Suggest you and he meet the team together to reset
What Good Looks Like (Outcome): Trust is rebuilt openly, team behaviour resets, return-to-work goes from fragile to stable
What Goes Wrong (If Poor Choice): Ryan disengages or relapses, team stays in tiptoe mode, silent erosion of his authority
